question.text: How does Nevada describe seat belts, and are they optional?

answer.text: Nevada calls seat belts your best protection against injury or death in a crash, and wearing them is required by law, not just advised.

teaching.text: In Nevada a seat belt is not a suggestion: the law requires it, and the handbook calls it your best protection in a crash. Remember: belts: best protection, required.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Nevada calls seat belts your best protection against injury or death in a crash, and wearing them is required by law, not just advised.

question.text: What share of Nevada highway deaths were unbelted drivers in the year the handbook cites?

answer.text: In two thousand twenty, drivers who were not wearing seat belts made up twenty-three point zero three percent of Nevada highway fatalities, an increase of one point one five percent over two thousand sixteen.

teaching.text: Unbelted drivers made up close to a quarter of Nevada highway deaths in the year cited, a share that grew over four years. Remember: nearly a quarter unbelted.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In two thousand twenty, drivers who were not wearing seat belts made up twenty-three point zero three percent of Nevada highway fatalities, an increase of one point one five percent over two thousand sixteen.

question.text: How many unbelted vehicle occupants died in Nevada over the five years the handbook cites?

answer.text: From two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty, three hundred forty-five unbelted vehicle occupants were killed in Nevada.

teaching.text: Hundreds of unbelted occupants died on Nevada roads over five years, which is why the belt law is taken seriously. Remember: hundreds lost without belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: From two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty, three hundred forty-five unbelted vehicle occupants were killed in Nevada.

question.text: Which seat belts must a car of model year nineteen sixty-eight or newer have?

answer.text: A car of model year nineteen sixty-eight or newer must have lap-type seat belts for the front-seat passengers.

teaching.text: Model year nineteen sixty-eight is the starting line for lap belts, and that first rule covers only the front-seat passengers. Remember: sixty-eight: front lap belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A car of model year nineteen sixty-eight or newer must have lap-type seat belts for the front-seat passengers.

question.text: Which seat belts must a car of model year nineteen seventy or newer have?

answer.text: A car of model year nineteen seventy or newer must have lap-type belts for every passenger plus shoulder harnesses for the front seat.

teaching.text: From nineteen seventy, every seat gets a lap belt and the front seat also gets shoulder harnesses. Remember: seventy: all laps, front shoulders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A car of model year nineteen seventy or newer must have lap-type belts for every passenger plus shoulder harnesses for the front seat.

question.text: How do the nineteen sixty-eight and nineteen seventy seat belt rules differ?

answer.text: Model year nineteen sixty-eight brought lap belts for front-seat passengers, while model year nineteen seventy brought lap belts for every passenger and front-seat shoulder harnesses.

teaching.text: Front lap belts came first in nineteen sixty-eight; belts for everyone plus front harnesses came in nineteen seventy. Remember: front first, then everyone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Model year nineteen sixty-eight brought lap belts for front-seat passengers, while model year nineteen seventy brought lap belts for every passenger and front-seat shoulder harnesses.

question.text: Who must wear a safety belt when the vehicle has one?

answer.text: The driver and every passenger aged six or older must wear a safety belt whenever the vehicle has one.

teaching.text: Everyone from age six up, driver included, buckles a belt whenever the vehicle has one. Remember: driver and six-plus buckle.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The driver and every passenger aged six or older must wear a safety belt whenever the vehicle has one.

question.text: Which children must ride in an approved child restraint system?

answer.text: Children under six, and children shorter than fifty-seven inches, must ride in an approved child restraint system (NRS 484B point one five seven).

teaching.text: A child under six, or a child under fifty-seven inches tall, rides in an approved child restraint system. Remember: under six or short.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children under six, and children shorter than fifty-seven inches, must ride in an approved child restraint system (NRS 484B point one five seven).

question.text: What penalties can follow for not restraining a young child?

answer.text: Failing to restrain a child under six or under fifty-seven inches can lead to fines, community service, a license suspension, or a combination of these.

teaching.text: Skipping a young child's restraint can mean fines, community service, a license suspension, or several at once. Remember: fines, service, suspension.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Failing to restrain a child under six or under fifty-seven inches can lead to fines, community service, a license suspension, or a combination of these.

question.text: How can the child restraint law affect the driver's own license?

answer.text: For children, the restraint law reaches the driver's license itself, since failing to restrain a young child can bring a license suspension as well as fines or community service.

teaching.text: The child restraint penalty can reach the driver's own license, not just the driver's wallet. Remember: unbuckled child, license risk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For children, the restraint law reaches the driver's license itself, since failing to restrain a young child can bring a license suspension as well as fines or community service.

question.text: How must a child under two ride?

answer.text: A child under two must ride in a rear-facing child restraint system in the back seat.

teaching.text: Children under two ride facing the rear, and they ride in the back seat. Remember: under two faces back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A child under two must ride in a rear-facing child restraint system in the back seat.

question.text: What two child-seating practices must you never use?

answer.text: Never hold a child on your lap or share one safety belt between a child and another person.

teaching.text: A lap is never a seat and a belt is never shared; every child needs separate protection. Remember: no laps, no sharing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never hold a child on your lap or share one safety belt between a child and another person.

question.text: What do age two, age six and the height rule each mark for child passengers?

answer.text: Age two marks the rear-facing back-seat rule, age six marks both the start of the adult belt requirement and the end of the under-six restraint rule, though a child still under fifty-seven inches keeps needing a restraint.

teaching.text: Age two sets the rear-facing rule, age six starts the adult belt rule, and height can keep a restraint in use after six. Remember: two, six, and height.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Age two marks the rear-facing back-seat rule, age six marks both the start of the adult belt requirement and the end of the under-six restraint rule, though a child still under fifty-seven inches keeps needing a restraint.

question.text: When is it illegal to leave a child seven or younger alone in a vehicle?

answer.text: Do not leave a child aged seven or younger alone in a vehicle when conditions pose a significant risk to the child's health and safety, unless a person at least twelve years old is supervising within sight (NRS two hundred two point four eight five).

teaching.text: A child seven or younger may not be left alone at significant risk unless someone at least twelve is watching within sight. Remember: never leave little ones.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not leave a child aged seven or younger alone in a vehicle when conditions pose a significant risk to the child's health and safety, unless a person at least twelve years old is supervising within sight (NRS two hundred two point four eight five).

question.text: What does Nevada law say about leaving a dog or cat in a hot or cold vehicle?

answer.text: Leaving a dog or cat unattended in a vehicle during extreme heat or cold is illegal, and police officers, firefighters and other officials are allowed to use reasonable force to free the animal (NRS two hundred two point four eight seven).

teaching.text: Dogs and cats may not be left in a vehicle in extreme heat or cold, and officials may use reasonable force to get them out. Remember: pets need rescue too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leaving a dog or cat unattended in a vehicle during extreme heat or cold is illegal, and police officers, firefighters and other officials are allowed to use reasonable force to free the animal (NRS two hundred two point four eight seven).

question.text: What kind of offense is breaking the unattended-child or unattended-pet law?

answer.text: Breaking the unattended-child or unattended-pet law is a misdemeanor.

teaching.text: Leaving a child or a pet unattended against the law is a misdemeanor in either case. Remember: misdemeanor for both.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Breaking the unattended-child or unattended-pet law is a misdemeanor.

question.text: Which ages matter in the unattended-child rule?

answer.text: The unattended-child rule protects children aged seven or younger, and the only exception is supervision by someone at least twelve years old who keeps the child in sight.

teaching.text: Two ages define the child rule: the child is seven or younger, and the person watching must be at least twelve. Remember: child seven, watcher twelve.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The unattended-child rule protects children aged seven or younger, and the only exception is supervision by someone at least twelve years old who keeps the child in sight.

question.text: How does the trigger for the unattended-child rule differ from the pet rule?

answer.text: The unattended-child rule turns on significant risk to the child's health and safety, while the dog-or-cat rule turns on extreme heat or cold; both are misdemeanors.

teaching.text: The child rule looks at significant risk to health and safety, while the pet rule looks at extreme heat or cold. Remember: risk for kids, weather for pets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The unattended-child rule turns on significant risk to the child's health and safety, while the dog-or-cat rule turns on extreme heat or cold; both are misdemeanors.

question.text: What do booster seats and belt-positioning seats do?

answer.text: Booster seats and belt-positioning seats raise or position a child so the vehicle's seat belt can secure the child safely.

teaching.text: A booster or belt-positioning seat lifts or positions the child so the car's own belt fits safely. Remember: boost so belts fit.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Booster seats and belt-positioning seats raise or position a child so the vehicle's seat belt can secure the child safely.

question.text: What two things should you check about a child restraint before travelling?

answer.text: Before travelling with a child, check that the restraint is approved by the US Department of Transportation under the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and suits the child's size and weight.

teaching.text: Check for US Department of Transportation approval under the federal standards, and match the seat to the child's size and weight. Remember: approved and right size.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before travelling with a child, check that the restraint is approved by the US Department of Transportation under the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and suits the child's size and weight.

question.text: How must a child restraint be installed?

answer.text: A child restraint must be installed safely and securely, following the manufacturer's instructions or another method approved by NHTSA.

teaching.text: Install the seat securely, following the maker's instructions or another method NHTSA approves. Remember: follow the maker's instructions.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A child restraint must be installed safely and securely, following the manufacturer's instructions or another method approved by NHTSA.

question.text: Which way do infants always face, and why?

answer.text: Infants are always buckled in facing the rear, because a rear-facing seat supports the baby's head and shields the neck and spine in most crashes.

teaching.text: Rear-facing seats cradle an infant's head and protect the neck and spine in most crashes. Remember: babies face the back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Infants are always buckled in facing the rear, because a rear-facing seat supports the baby's head and shields the neck and spine in most crashes.

question.text: How does a booster seat differ from a rear-facing infant seat?

answer.text: A booster or belt-positioning seat works with the vehicle's own seat belt, while a rear-facing seat holds the infant itself and protects the head, neck and spine.

teaching.text: A booster relies on the vehicle belt, while a rear-facing seat holds and protects the infant directly. Remember: booster uses belt, infant seat holds.

question.text: What three checks make child travel safe?

answer.text: Safe child travel needs three checks: a DOT-approved restraint, a seat that fits the child's size and weight, and an installation that follows the manufacturer or NHTSA.

teaching.text: Three checks before any trip: approved seat, right fit for the child, and correct installation. Remember: approved, fitted, installed right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Safe child travel needs three checks: a DOT-approved restraint, a seat that fits the child's size and weight, and an installation that follows the manufacturer or NHTSA.

question.text: Where is the safest place for children to ride, and what if an older child must sit in front?

answer.text: The back seat is generally the safest place for children; an older child who must ride in front should have the vehicle seat moved as far back as it goes.

teaching.text: Children ride safest in back; if an older child must sit in front, slide that seat all the way back. Remember: kids in back, seat back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The back seat is generally the safest place for children; an older child who must ride in front should have the vehicle seat moved as far back as it goes.

question.text: How do you keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag?

answer.text: To keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag, use a restraint with a full harness or a properly fitted shoulder and lap belt.

teaching.text: A full harness or a well-fitted shoulder and lap belt keeps a child's head out of the airbag's path. Remember: harness or fitted belt.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag, use a restraint with a full harness or a properly fitted shoulder and lap belt.

question.text: Who can be badly hurt by an airbag even in a minor collision?

answer.text: Passengers who are unbuckled or sitting too close to an airbag can be badly hurt even in a minor collision or a sudden stop.

teaching.text: Airbags can badly hurt passengers who are unbuckled or sitting too close, even in a small crash or a sudden stop. Remember: unbuckled or too close.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passengers who are unbuckled or sitting too close to an airbag can be badly hurt even in a minor collision or a sudden stop.

question.text: Why must an infant never ride in front of a passenger-side airbag?

answer.text: Never place an infant in the front seat of a car that has a passenger-side airbag, because the airbag bursts out of the dashboard at two hundred miles per hour and can strike the back of the baby's head through the safety seat.

teaching.text: A passenger airbag deploys with enough speed to hit the back of a baby's head through the seat, so infants never ride in front of one. Remember: no baby before airbag.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never place an infant in the front seat of a car that has a passenger-side airbag, because the airbag bursts out of the dashboard at two hundred miles per hour and can strike the back of the baby's head through the safety seat.

question.text: How do the front-seat rules differ for an older child and an infant?

answer.text: Older children may ride up front only when necessary and with the seat pushed fully back, but an infant may never ride in front of a passenger-side airbag.

teaching.text: An older child may ride in front when necessary with the seat pushed back, but an infant never rides in front of a passenger airbag. Remember: older maybe, infant never.
